source.title: Selective Steering: Norm-Preserving Control Through Discriminative Layer Selection

record.tranche_reason: The study extracts a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means feature and tests whether rotating activations using it changes harmful-request compliance and preserves benchmark performance. This is a different intervention from the original all-layer ablation and addition.
record.gate_note: The study reports steering effects on harmful prompts, refusal scores, and general-capability benchmarks. Its ablation figures and intermediate activation statistics are not recorded as separate rows here when they serve as selection or calibration evidence rather than a distinct reported behavioral outcome. Other evaluator results and method-ablation comparisons are omitted under the row limit; see rows_left_out.
record.test_reason: The study extracts a harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction and steers along it with norm-preserving rotation at selected layers. It reports harmful-request compliance (HarmBench ASR), substring refusal scores, and capability retention across 8 instruct models. This is a different intervention aimed at the V1 question of whether this direction mediates refusal while other abilities are kept. It also reports Arditi-style directional ablation (DirAbl) as a baseline.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that norm-preserving rotation restricted to discriminative layers (opposite-signed class-mean projections) gives controllable harmful compliance, with no perplexity-threshold violations and near-full benchmark retention. They say both components are necessary, per their ablations. They float the Gemma two-peak pattern as possibly reflecting multiple refusal-related directions or a suboptimal diff-in-means direction. Note: the text says nine models but evaluates eight.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means feature, but steers by norm-preserving rotation in a two-dimensional plane and applies it only at selected discriminative layers. It does not perform the original all-layer, all-position ablation or addition.
record.method_sensitivity: The method selects discriminative layers and the angle maximizing HarmBench ASR. Angle-response curves differ by architecture; Gemma models are described as having two peaks. The authors also report sensitivity of alternative angular-steering methods to layer selection and norm preservation, but those comparisons are not extracted as rows here.
record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The behavioral evaluation uses 104 held-out AdvBench prompts. Refusal is detected by substring matching, and the study notes evaluator-specific issues, especially PolyGuard's tendency to score degraded text as unsafe. The study does not directly test the original all-layer ablation/addition claim. Uncertainty is not stated for the extracted ASR, refusal, or benchmark-accuracy results.
record.rows_left_out: Within the 60-row limit, omitted the PolyGuard and Qwen2.5-14B judge values in Table 1, the layer-selection and norm-preservation ablation results in Appendix E (Tables 5–6), and additional coherence metrics in Table 4. These are method/evaluator comparisons or generation-quality measures rather than the principal direct behavior and capability outcomes extracted above.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal on harmless prompts. Full all-layer, all-position ablation as in the original is tested only as the DirAbl baseline, with unclear implementation.
No direct comparison of single versus multi-direction or cone representations. The Gemma bimodal peaks are only interpretive.
No jailbreak mechanism or adversarial-training test.

missing.what: DirAbl (Arditi directional ablation) baseline: HarmBench/LLM-judge ASR and refusal score per model. For example, Llama-3.1-8B refusal is 0.5288 and Qwen2.5-1.5B is 0.6250, while Qwen2.5-3B is 0.0192. Benchmark accuracy under DirAbl is largely kept.

Layer-selection ablation with norm-preserving rotation. Early or random-half layers leave refusal at about 0.97–0.99, and late layers at 0.69–0.95. Uniform all-layer rotation drives substring refusal to about 0 but gives only 0.28–0.55 HarmBench ASR, with coherence cost. This covers Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B and Gemma-2-9B.
Coherence metrics under DirAbl versus other methods. DirAbl n-gram repetition is low and its compression ratio is moderate.

record.verdict_notes: This is a method paper about steering quality; its V1 relevance comes from using the diff-in-means refusal direction. The best angles are chosen by maximising ASR, apparently on the evaluation prompts. Refusal is measured by substring matching, and the no-steering refusal score is not reported. I dropped the reader's V4 'supports' label because the two-peak observation is speculative and figure-only.

versions.untested_parts: Does not ablate the direction at every layer and position or add it to induce refusals on harmless requests. The intervention is selective, norm-preserving rotation, not the original removal/addition procedure.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration.
Does not test whether existing jailbreaks suppress the direction or whether training against its ablation adds robustness.
The study does not directly compare affine, cone, or multi-direction representations; its evidence is an interpretation of angle-response curves for Gemma models.
Does not separate harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
No cross-language, base-to-instruct, or model-variant transfer test.
Does not vary refusal training or its timing.

relationships.reason: HarmBench ASR rises from 0–0.07 to 0.68–0.88 (r01–r08). Substring refusal is 0 in seven models and 0.09 in one (r09–r16). tinyBenchmarks accuracy stays within about 0.06 of no steering (r17–r56).

relation.reason: Its own interventions on the diff-in-means direction, both SS and the DirAbl baseline, yield refusal and ASR numbers that bear on whether the direction mediates refusal.

tranche.reason: It steers along a harmful-minus-harmless diff-in-means direction with a different intervention (norm-preserving rotation at selected layers). It reports refusal rate, harmful compliance and capability, and also runs Arditi-style DirAbl as a baseline. Its results bear on V1.

source_check.notes: The abstract and conclusion say nine models, but all tables cover eight. Best angles are chosen per method to maximise HarmBench ASR on the same 104 AdvBench eval prompts; no validation split is stated. The text writes DirAbl with the study's d_feat (the max inter-layer cosine candidate), and its layer scope is unstated. On Gemma, DirAbl gives low refusal (0.02/0.08) but HarmBench ASR of only 0.25/0.12. No uncertainty is given for ASR, refusal or accuracy, so the record's uncertainty=y is doubtful.

statements.correction: arXiv:2601.19375: rotation in a 2D plane (b1 = diff-in-means, b2 = PCA component) applied only at layers with opposite-signed class-mean projections. Angle chosen per method for max HarmBench ASR on the 104-prompt AdvBench eval set. Its DirAbl baseline (Table 1) leaves substring refusal 0.5288/0.2019/0.2404/0.6250 on Llama-3.1-8B/3.2-1B/3.2-3B/Qwen2.5-1.5B. No CIs or std on ASR, refusal or accuracy; ± std appears only on Table 4 coherence metrics, across angles. Text is arXiv v1 with no venue stated.
statements.problem: The numbers for this study are right, but the opening sentence groups it with removal by the original's code or an all-layer projection. Its numbers come from norm-preserving rotation at selected discriminative layers. Its own DirAbl (projection) baseline removed refusal only partly on 4 of 8 models. 'uncertainty y' is overstated, and the text never states the ACL venue.

statements.correction: Table 1 DirAbl: HarmBench 0.3269 (Llama-3.1-8B), 0.5481 (Llama-3.2-1B), 0.5385 (Llama-3.2-3B), 0.2500 (Qwen2.5-1.5B). Refusal 0.5288, 0.2019, 0.2404, 0.6250. Qwen2.5-3B/7B: refusal 0.0192/0.0577, HarmBench 0.5288/0.5577. gemma-2-2b/9b: refusal 0.0192/0.0769, HarmBench only 0.2500/0.1154. No-steering Llama-3.1-8B HarmBench ASR 0.0577 (Table 2). Eval set: the remaining 20% of AdvBench, 104 prompts.
statements.problem: The DirAbl HarmBench ASR range for the four named models is 0.25–0.55, not 0.25–0.56 (0.56 is Qwen2.5-7B's 0.5577). 'Refusal down to' has no stated baseline, because Table 1 has no No Steering row. The text does not say which layers DirAbl is applied at.

statements.correction: arXiv:2601.19375: HarmBench ASR 0.00–0.07 -> 0.68–0.88 under Selective Steering (rotation at discriminative layers, best-ASR angle), not projection or weight edit. Its controls are layer-subset ablations (random 50%/early/late/all layers) on 3 models (Table 5) plus baseline methods, not a random direction. Its own DirAbl baseline leaves refusal 0.20–0.63 on 4/8 models.
statements.problem: The study is cited as evidence that removal by all-layer projection or weight edit is strongest beside a random or orthogonal control. This study uses selected-layer rotation, has no random-direction control, and gives no uncertainty on its main metrics. The text does not state ACL.
